transcript.text: Our Dyson (one of the V ones, purple bits) keeps cutting out after about 5-10 seconds. Not every time - some days it does a whole room fine. It's maybe 5 years old. Already cleaned the filter and checked for blockages. Battery or something else?

At five years old, my money is on the battery, but there's one other common cause worth ruling out first. Why the battery: a Dyson V battery of that age often still shows charge, but its cells can't deliver the current the motor needs. The voltage dips under load, the electronics see that as a flat or faulty battery, and the motor stops after a few seconds. It's often worse in boost/max mode or with the motorised floorhead fitted, and it can come and go with how charged and how warm the battery is. That fits 'some days fine, some days not'. The usual airflow causes are mostly ruled out. The main alternative is the floorhead. A brush bar that's tangled or stiff makes the machine cut out to protect itself. 1. Charge it fully, then use it on normal (not boost/max) with just the crevice tool on the wand, no floorhead. If it still cuts out within seconds, it's probably the battery.
2. If it runs fine like that, switch it off, turn the floorhead over and cut away any hair or thread on the brush bar and end caps. Check the bar spins freely by hand. If it was stiff or tangled, that was your cut-out.
3. Watch how it cuts out. Stopping dead points to the battery. Pulsing on and off points to airflow, often a filter that wasn't fully dry. After washing, a filter needs a full 24 hours to dry. If step 1 points to the battery, a replacement battery is the likely fix. On most V models it's an owner-fit job held by a couple of screws or a clip. That's usually well worth doing rather than replacing the vacuum, as long as the motor and body are otherwise fine. If it still cuts out with a good battery and a clear floorhead, the fault is in the motor or its electronics, which is a job for Dyson or a repairer. When it cuts out, does it stop dead or pulse? And does it still cut out with just a tool on the wand?

It stops dead, no pulsing. In handheld mode with no tool it still cuts out sometimes, just less often. On Max it nearly always stops within a few seconds. No smell, and the battery isn't swollen or hot.

That pattern points firmly at the battery. I'd put it at fairly high confidence, but I'm not certain yet. Here's why. It still happens in handheld mode with no tool, so it isn't the floorhead. Max mode makes it far worse, and Max is exactly what draws the most current from tired cells. Five years is also about when these batteries typically give up. The battery not being swollen or hot is reassuring for safety, but it doesn't rule this out. A worn pack usually looks completely normal. 1. If the battery indicator flashes or shows low charge even though it has just come off the charger, that's the battery protection tripping, which all but suggests it. A distinct fault symbol (on models with a screen) or no lights at all is less typical and worth telling me about.
2. With it switched off, check the battery is held firmly. On most V models it's fixed by a screw or two or a clip, and these can work loose. Make sure it doesn't wobble, and wipe the metal contacts clean and dry. A loose or dirty connection can also cause a dead stop, and it's a free fix. If it was loose and tightening it cures the problem, you're done. The definitive test is to try a known-good battery, if you can borrow one from a friend's compatible Dyson. If it runs normally on that, even on Max, that proves the battery is the fault. If it still cuts out on a good battery, the motor or its electronics are more likely, and that's a job for Dyson or a repairer. In that case it's worth checking whether a repair is economical at this age. If it does turn out to be the battery, it's normally an owner-fit job and well worth doing on an otherwise healthy machine. Stick to a genuine or reputable battery, as cheap unbranded packs are a known fire risk. What do the lights do when it stops?
Sometimes the blue lights flash a few times when it stops, sometimes nothing at all. No spare battery to swap-test, sorry. Is it worth spending £60+ on a new battery then?

[Heading: Likely cause: battery — flat or failed (cordless)]
In most cases, yes, it's worth it, as long as the rest of the machine is in good shape: decent suction when it does run, no grinding or burning smell, and an undamaged body and bin. A battery is the part that wears out on these, and replacing it usually gives you several more years of use. A new cordless of similar spec will typically cost several times what a battery does. It's less worth it if the machine is also cracked or worn elsewhere, or if you were already thinking of upgrading. Blue lights flashing a few times as it stops is typically the battery protection cutting in. Stopping with no lights at all fits too, because a tired pack's voltage can collapse so fast the indicator doesn't get a chance. 1. If you haven't already, switch it off, check the battery is screwed or clipped in tight with no wobble, and wipe the contacts clean and dry. It's free, and a loose connection can mimic a failing battery.
2. Buy a genuine Dyson battery or one from a reputable brand with a proper warranty. Cheap unbranded packs are a known fire risk. A genuine one also protects you if it turns out not to be the battery after all. If a new battery doesn't cure it, the motor or its electronics are next in line, and that's one for Dyson or a repairer. To make sure you get the right battery, can you find the model number? It's usually on a sticker on the body, often under the bin or near where the battery fits. If it's awkward to get to right now, that can wait.
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
I checked the label under the bin and it says SV11. Can you confirm which battery that needs and whether £60+ is a fair price?

[Heading: Likely cause: battery — flat or failed (cordless)]
I can't confirm exactly which battery your machine takes from SV11 alone. Dyson uses codes like that as a model type, and the same code can cover more than one version or region, with different batteries. I also don't have a confirmed parts match for it, so I'd rather not guess and have you buy the wrong one. The reliable way to get the right one:
1. Look on the same label under the bin for the full serial number. It's usually a longer string of letters and numbers, often with "UK" in it.
2. Enter it on Dyson's website (spares or support section), or give it to Dyson's helpline. They'll show the exact genuine battery for your machine and its current price.
3. If you buy from a third-party seller, check that their listing names your exact model and version, not just "fits V-series". Choose a reputable brand with a proper warranty. On price, I can't tell you what's fair right now, because it changes and depends on the seller. A good rule is to compare against Dyson's own price for your serial number. A genuine or well-reviewed branded battery costing somewhere near that is normal. A pack far cheaper than that is a warning sign, as unbranded batteries are a known fire risk. Either way, a battery is usually a fraction of the cost of a new cordless, so it's still the sensible repair if the rest of the machine is sound. If you'd rather not do it yourself, Dyson or a local vacuum repairer can supply and fit the right battery for you. If a new battery doesn't cure the cutting out, the motor or electronics would be next, and that's a job for them anyway.
